lede: Push something heavy and it shifts slowly; push something light with the same effort and it shoots away. Newton's second law puts a number on that, and Unit 2 asks you to use it on bodies sliding along the ground and on lifts hanging from a cable.
can: Find the resultant force along the line of motion and use it in $F = ma$
Tell the mass from the weight, and put each one where it belongs
Handle a resistance given as so many newtons per kilogram

text: Force, mass and the motion that follows

md: Forces do not make things move at a steady speed; they make things change speed. The bigger the resultant force and the lighter the body, the faster that change happens, and one short equation says exactly how much.

md:
$F = ma$ is on the Unit 2 sheet, and the $F$ is the **resultant** along the line of motion. Here that is $40 - 12 = 28$ N.

Then $28 = 7a$ gives $a = 4$ m/s². The dashed arrow marks the acceleration, and it is deliberately drawn differently: it is not a force.

prompt: A body is pushed by 60 N against a resistance of 20 N. What resultant force goes into $F = ma$, in newtons?
explain: $60 - 20 = 40$ N. The resistance acts backwards, so it comes off the driving force.

text: 2. Mass in the equation, weight on the diagram

alt: A table comparing mass and weight: mass is how much matter there is, 7 kilograms, and it is what goes into F = ma; weight is the pull of gravity on it, 7 times 10 equals 70 newtons, and it is what goes on the diagram.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 434 210' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='434' height='210'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='2' y='2' width='430' height='206' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><text x='12' y='35' text-anchor='start' font-size='13.5' font-weight='600'>The two numbers a body carries</text><text x='12' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>Mass</text><text x='213' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>Weight</text><text x='12' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>how much matter there is</text><text x='213' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the pull of gravity on it</text><text x='12' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>7 kg</text><text x='213' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>7 × 10 = 70 N</text><text x='12' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>goes into F = ma</text><text x='213' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>goes on the diagram</text><text x='12' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>never changes</text><text x='213' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>changes if g changes</text><path d='M6 76H428M6 106H428M6 136H428M6 166H428M6 196H428M207 46V196' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/></g></svg>
caption: Two numbers, two jobs, and only one of them belongs in the equation.

md:
A mass of $7$ kg has a weight of $7 \times 10 = 70$ N, and that weight is the arrow pointing down on the diagram.

The $m$ in $F = ma$ is the mass, in kilograms. Putting the weight there makes every acceleration ten times too small; it is the slip the reports name most often here.

title: Why the two cannot be swapped
md: Mass measures how much matter there is; weight measures how hard gravity pulls on it. $F = ma$ asks how hard a body is to accelerate, and that depends on the matter — so the mass belongs in it. The weight enters only when gravity is one of the forces acting.

prompt: A block of mass 5 kg, weight 50 N, feels a resultant force of 30 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: $30 = 5a$, so $a = 6$ m/s². Dividing by 50 would use the weight, and give 0.6.

alt: A table of the four lines to write every time: name the body, write the resultant as the driving force minus the resistance, set that resultant equal to mass times acceleration, then give the answer with its units.

caption: The layout that keeps one body's forces separate from another's.

md:
Start by naming the body: *for the crate:*. Examiners report forces on one body being mixed with forces on a whole system, and that one phrase is what stops it.

Then the resultant, then the equation, then the answer with its unit. The equation of motion is a method mark that survives an arithmetic slip, so it is worth writing down even when the numbers look hard.

title: Newton's 2nd Law of Motion, F = ma
why: The same law at a slower pace, with the resultant formed before anything else. It is an A level video, so stop before any coefficient of friction appears: CCEA never uses one.

prompt: A crate of mass 12 kg is dragged by 90 N against a resistance of 30 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?

alt: A table showing how a resistance of 3 newtons per kilogram on a crate of 8 kilograms becomes a single force of 24 newtons, and a note that it is not a coefficient of friction.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 442 210' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='442' height='210'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='2' y='2' width='438' height='206' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><text x='12' y='35' text-anchor='start' font-size='13.5' font-weight='600'>A resistance given per kilogram</text><text x='12' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>What the stem says</text><text x='161' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>What it means</text><text x='12' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>3 N per kg</text><text x='161' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>every kilogram is resisted by 3 N</text><text x='12' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the crate is 8 kg</text><text x='161' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>so the resistance is 3 × 8</text><text x='12' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the force to use</text><text x='161' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>24 N</text><text x='12' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>what it is not</text><text x='161' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>a coefficient of friction</text><path d='M6 76H436M6 106H436M6 136H436M6 166H436M6 196H436M155 46V196' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/></g></svg>
caption: A rate, a mass, and the single force they make.

md:
CCEA never tests $F = \mu R$. Friction arrives either as a plain value or as **so many newtons per kilogram**, and the second form is a one-step conversion: multiply by the mass.

A crate of $8$ kg with $3$ N per kg feels $3 \times 8 = 24$ N of resistance. It looks like a coefficient and it is not one.

prompt: A resistance of 5 N per kg acts on a body of mass 9 kg. What is the resisting force, in newtons?
explain: $5 \times 9 = 45$ N. Every kilogram is resisted by 5 N, and there are 9 of them.

alt: A lift of mass 500 kilograms hanging on a cable, with the tension of 5600 newtons acting upwards and the weight of 5000 newtons downwards, and an open arrow marking the acceleration upwards.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 470 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='470' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='187' y='112' width='96' height='56' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='235' y='145' text-anchor='middle' font-size='13' font-weight='600'>500 kg</text><path d='M235 112L235 34' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M235 34L238.8 43L231.2 43Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='235' y='18' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>T = 5600 N</text><path d='M235 168L235 246' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M235 246L231.2 237L238.8 237Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='235' y='262' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>5000 N</text><path d='M340 142L340 78' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M340 78l-5 9M340 78l5 9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><text x='348' y='86' text-anchor='start' font-size='12'>a</text><text x='235' y='290' text-anchor='middle' font-size='11.5'>up is positive, so the resultant is T − mg</text></g></svg>
caption: Tension up, weight down, and a resultant of $600$ N.

md:
Vertical motion is the same equation with the weight in it. Choose a direction, say so, and write the resultant in that direction.

**Up positive:** $5600 - 5000 = 500a$, so $a = 1.2$ m/s². The answer is positive, so the acceleration is upwards. A negative answer would simply mean downwards.

task: On the Acceleration screen, set friction to zero and apply a known force to a known mass. Predict the acceleration from $F = ma$ before you release, then check the readout. Turn friction on and predict again: the resultant is now the applied force minus the friction. The model is horizontal only, so it says nothing about the lift.

prompt: A lift of mass 300 kg hangs on a cable with tension 3300 N. Taking up as positive, which equation is right?
explain: The weight is $300 \times 10 = 3000$ N, and it acts downwards against the tension. Leaving it out, or subtracting the mass instead, are the two usual slips.

caption: The mass is the unknown, so the equation has to be built around it.

md:
When a part prints the answer and says *show that*, the marks are for getting there forwards: write the resultant, set it equal to $Ma$, collect the $M$ terms and solve.

Substituting the printed value back in and checking both sides agree is **capped at two marks** by CCEA, because it assumes what you were asked to prove.

prompt: A part says 'Show that the mass is 650 kg'. Which route earns full marks?
options: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
Putting 650 into the equation and showing both sides agree
Writing down 650 kg with its units
answer: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
explain: Verification is capped at two marks; the printed answer is the last line you write, never the first.

md:
Form the resultant along the line of motion before using $F = ma$.
Put the mass in the equation and the weight on the diagram.
Turn a resistance given per kilogram into a single force.
Write and solve the equation for a lift, and say which way it accelerates.
Derive a 'show that' forwards rather than verifying it.

This sits inside a multi-part mechanics question, often the last one: a resistance or a resultant for 2 marks, then $F = ma$ for 3, then a constant-acceleration formula. The first mark is the equation of motion with the right numbers in it; the last is the value with its unit. Stuck? Write *for the [body]:*, then the resultant, and the method mark is already yours.
